975.bp: Spotify has to decide which podcast ad or in-app promotion to show to a listener at a particular moment. The ordinary-world problem is matching scarce listener attention with podcast creators and advertisers who want real listening, not just an impression that vanishes. This is especially painful for new ad objectives and less-streamed podcasts, because the system has little direct evidence about who will click, stream, or follow after seeing them. A large platform already observes many interactions among users, podcast content, context, and creative material, but those observations are often split across advertising and promotion pipelines. This paper tries to turn that scattered history into a shared targeting system. The goal is practical: lower the cost of producing an actual podcast stream, raise stream rates, support different business goals, and avoid rebuilding a separate model whenever a new low-data targeting task appears.
975.wh: The hard part is that the system must personalize before it has much evidence for the thing being personalized. A popular podcast campaign can reveal its audience quickly because many users see it and respond. A new objective, a new promotion type, or a less-streamed podcast may have only a thin trail of clicks, streams, or follows. If the model waits for enough direct examples, the campaign wastes money while learning. If it guesses too broadly, listeners see irrelevant promotions and the platform pays for attention that does not become listening. The paper also faces a second tension: ads and promotions may share useful behavior patterns, but they are not identical business tasks. A model must learn common structure without pretending that a click, a stream, and a follow are the same event. It must also stay maintainable inside a real advertising system, where separate historical pipelines can become costly silos.
975.naive: A smart beginner would build one predictor for each advertising or promotion goal. One model would estimate clicks, another streams, another follows, and each new campaign or objective would train mostly from its own history. That feels clean because each model has a narrow job. It fails when data is scarce. A new podcast promotion may not have enough past outcomes to teach a reliable rule, and a less-streamed podcast may look unimportant simply because it has had little exposure. The separate-model approach also throws away transferable clues, such as which user contexts tend to lead to podcast listening or which creative features tend to attract attention. Operationally, it multiplies systems that must be monitored, updated, and debugged.
975.ap: The core idea is to learn many related targeting tasks together so that a new or low-data task can borrow experience from older, larger ones. The paper calls this multi-task learning, which here means one joint model is trained to care about several outcomes at once instead of treating every goal as a separate island. It also uses transfer learning, meaning patterns learned from large-scale ad and content interactions are reused when a newer task lacks its own history. The shared part of the model reads user, content, context, and creative features and forms a common description useful across ads and promotions. Task-specific parts can then aim at streams, clicks, follows, or in-app promotion goals. The central move is not just sharing a database; it is making the prediction machinery itself share what is generally useful while still allowing different objectives to pull in different directions.
975.mech: The mechanism starts with events from Spotify's podcast ecosystem. Each event can include who the listener is in broad feature form, what podcast or content is being promoted, what context surrounds the opportunity, what creative material is shown, and what outcome follows, such as a stream, click, or follow. These examples enter a single joint training process. First, the model learns a shared internal description of the situation from all feature groups together. In plain terms, it tries to compress many clues into reusable signals: listener tendency, content appeal, contextual fit, and creative quality. Second, several objective heads read that shared description and each estimate a different outcome. During training, errors from all objectives update the shared part, so evidence from a click task or an ancillary outcome can improve the common understanding used by a stream task. Third, when a new advertising objective or low-data promotion arrives, Spotify can either apply the joint model directly or fine-tune it with the limited new examples. At serving time, the system scores candidate ads or promotions for the listener and context, balancing the relevant objectives for the business goal. The output is a targeting decision that aims to create valuable podcast outcomes while using one maintainable model family rather than many isolated pipelines.
975.math: The main mathematical idea is shared statistical learning under scarce evidence. The model sees repeated cases where features came before outcomes, and it estimates which patterns make streams, clicks, or follows more likely. Because any one new task has too few examples, the important trick is to pool information across related tasks without collapsing them into one task. Multi-task learning does this by giving tasks a common middle layer and separate output layers. The common layer learns reusable structure, while the separate outputs let each objective define its own kind of error. Optimization, in this setting, means defining what counts as wrong for each outcome and repeatedly changing the model's controllable settings to reduce the combined wrongness. Transfer learning adds another mathematical bet: patterns learned from high-volume ad and content interactions will still be informative for a new objective. The tradeoff is sharing versus specificity. Too little sharing leaves cold-start tasks starved; too much sharing lets dominant tasks drown out smaller ones. The shared user, content, context, and creative description is useful only if those feature groups carry real similarities across ads and promotions. Ancillary objectives matter because a weaker or indirect signal can still teach the shared layer when the main stream signal is sparse.
975.dots: This paper sits squarely in the conference's cold-start recommendation thread: how to recommend or target something before the system has enough direct behavior for it. Nearby recommendation papers in the same batch attack related pressure from different sides. DDGCL focuses on long-tail items in a user-item graph, using broader structure to help rare items. RankID tries to make a unified identifier from different feature types for large-scale recommendation. ARROW asks how language-model reasoning can explain recommendation decisions. The Spotify paper is more production-facing: it connects cold-start, ranking, multiple business objectives, and maintainability in one advertising system. It also touches the recurring theme of transfer across tasks. The deeper shared problem is choosing a small action from many candidates under uncertainty, where the system must use old evidence without letting old popularity decide the future for every new podcast.
975.ww: The approach should work better than the naive split because listener behavior contains reusable regularities. A person who responds to one podcast promotion is not a blank slate for every other podcast campaign; their interests, listening context, and response to creative material can carry over. Likewise, a podcast with little history may still have content features that resemble podcasts with known audiences. By training tasks together, the shared part of the model sees more examples and can learn these broad relationships before a new objective appears. The separate objectives then prevent the system from treating every success signal as identical. A click may show curiosity, a stream shows actual listening, and a follow suggests longer-term interest. Learning them together can make the common description richer, while the task-specific outputs preserve the difference among goals. The reported online A/B tests support this intuition: lower effective cost per stream and higher stream rates indicate that the system is not merely predicting more activity, but improving the practical match between promotions and listeners, especially where sparse history normally hurts.
975.po: The payoff is a more useful and simpler targeting system for Spotify podcasts. The abstract reports up to a 22 percent reduction in effective Cost-Per-Stream, with particularly strong benefit for less-streamed podcasts, and an 18 to 24 percent increase in podcast stream rates. It also says offline experiments and ablations show that ancillary objectives and feature groups contribute to cold-start performance. Beyond the measured gains, the unified model improves coverage and maintainability because ads and promotions no longer need to live in historically separate targeting pipelines.
975.limits: The claims depend on ads and promotions sharing enough behavioral structure for transfer to help. If a new objective attracts a very different audience, uses unusual creative material, or measures success in a way unrelated to past podcast outcomes, the shared model could transfer the wrong lessons. The abstract reports online A/B tests and offline ablations, but it does not specify the experimental duration, audience segments, objective weighting, fairness effects across creators, or long-term listener satisfaction. Multi-objective systems also require choices about which goals matter most. Better cost per stream may still hide tradeoffs among advertiser value, user experience, and exposure for different kinds of podcasts.

976.bp: This tutorial is about systems made of connected parts whose connections and behavior change together. In a social network, a person's opinion can alter who they talk to, and those new conversations can then alter later opinions. In a brain, activity can reshape neural connections, and those changed connections affect future activity. The same pattern appears in disease spread, power grids, and other networked systems: the map of relationships is not just a background drawing, because the map helps decide what happens next. The practical need is prediction and safety under partial knowledge. A planner may want to know whether an outbreak will grow, whether a power system will stay reliable, whether a group will synchronize, or whether a small failure can cascade. The tutorial's subject is how to reason when the network, its strengths, its rules of change, and outside pressures are all partly unknown.
976.wh: The hard part is that uncertainty enters through several doors at once. One edge may be missing, another may have the wrong strength, a node may react differently than expected, and an outside influence may change over time. In an ordinary static network, a wrong link can already distort the answer. In a dynamical network, the error can feed forward: a slightly wrong contact pattern can change a disease forecast, that forecast can change an intervention, and the intervention can change the later network. The abstract points to fluctuating edge weights, evolving connections, stochastic interactions, unknown contact patterns, changing transmission rates, uncertain demand, and renewable energy variation. These are not small bookkeeping errors. They change stability, synchronization, and cascading failure questions because those outcomes depend on how local changes travel through the whole connected system over time.
976.naive: A smart beginner might first draw the best available network, choose one set of parameters, run the model once, and treat the answer as the forecast. That is natural because it turns a messy situation into a single map and a single future. It fails because the single map is often only a guess. Unknown contacts in epidemiology, changing neural links, fluctuating edge weights, and variable power demand can all produce different futures from nearly the same starting picture. Another beginner move is to test a few hand-picked alternatives, but that still misses which uncertainties matter most and how combinations of small errors can amplify each other.
976.ap: The core idea is to make the unknown parts of the dynamical network visible instead of hiding them inside one confident forecast. Uncertainty quantification means naming the pieces that are not known exactly, describing how much they may vary, and tracing how that variation changes the predicted behavior. The tutorial bridges two objects: a network whose nodes and links shape a dynamic process, and a disciplined way to measure uncertainty in model structure, parameters, and outside inputs. Mechanically, this means treating the network not as one fixed diagram but as a family of plausible diagrams and rules. The important question then changes from, What will happen? to, What range of behavior is plausible, which uncertain pieces drive that range, and how reliable is the conclusion about stability, synchronization, or failure spread?
976.mech: The mechanism starts with a dynamical network description. The inputs are the nodes, the links among them, the strengths or weights of those links, the rules by which activity changes over time, and outside influences such as contact rates, demand, or renewable energy supply. First, the analyst separates what is known from what is uncertain. A link may exist with uncertain strength, a connection may appear or disappear, a transmission rate may vary, or an external load may fluctuate. Second, those uncertainties are represented as ranges, chances, or alternative scenarios, depending on what evidence is available. Third, the dynamic model is run or analyzed across those possibilities so the uncertainty can move through the system rather than remain a note in the margin. Fourth, the outputs are compared: some versions may settle, some may synchronize, some may trigger cascades, and some may make predictions unreliable. Finally, the analyst asks which uncertain inputs changed the outcome most. The result is not just a predicted trajectory. It is a map from uncertain network structure, uncertain parameters, and uncertain outside pressure to a set of possible behaviors and a measure of how much confidence the decision maker should place in each conclusion.
976.math: The main mathematical objects are a graph, a time rule, and a measured description of uncertainty. The graph is the map: nodes stand for people, neurons, power components, or other units, and links stand for channels through which influence, activity, infection, or load can pass. The time rule says how the state of each node changes as its own condition, its neighbors, and outside forces change. Dynamical systems is the name for studying such rules over time: instead of asking only what the network looks like now, it asks where the whole connected system can move next and whether it settles, oscillates, synchronizes, or breaks. Probability enters because the analyst does not know every link, parameter, or outside shock exactly. It turns incomplete evidence into explicit degrees of belief or ranges of plausible values. Sensitivity analysis is the related idea of asking which uncertain knob matters most: if a small change in one transmission rate greatly changes an outbreak forecast, that knob deserves attention. The tradeoff is detail versus trust. A single forecast is easy to read but can hide fragility; a quantified range is harder to summarize but better matches a world where the map and the process are both uncertain.
976.dots: This tutorial sits where several recurring conference ideas meet. It is a network paper because the object of study is a set of connected units where neighbors carry influence. It is also a probability paper because the central problem is acting with incomplete, noisy, and changing evidence. It connects to time-series and spatiotemporal work because the answer depends on how signals evolve, not just on a one-time snapshot. It also touches reliability and anomaly concerns: cascading failures in power systems and uncertain outbreaks are cases where wrong confidence can be costly. Compared with graph learning papers that spread evidence through a fixed relationship map, this topic asks what happens when the map itself, the strengths on the links, and the external pressures are uncertain. Compared with ordinary forecasting papers, it keeps the connected structure visible while forecasting.
976.ww: The approach works because it matches the shape of the real problem. In a dynamical network, uncertainty is not an afterthought added after prediction; it is one of the forces that determines the prediction. If unknown contact patterns are treated as fixed, an epidemic model may look precise while being wrong for the reason that matters most. If renewable supply is treated as a known number, a power reliability assessment can miss the cases where demand and generation move in an unlucky combination. By pushing uncertain inputs through the same network dynamics that produce the forecast, uncertainty quantification shows where confidence is justified and where it is fragile. It also helps separate harmless noise from dangerous uncertainty. Some link-weight variation may barely affect synchronization, while a small change in a key bridge link may change whether a cascade spreads. That distinction is exactly what a one-run model cannot reveal. The method is useful because it turns ignorance into an object that can be inspected, compared, and reduced.
976.po: The payoff is a clearer way to study adaptive social networks, neural plasticity, epidemiology, power systems, and similar connected systems when the available knowledge is incomplete or noisy. The abstract promises a tutorial that gives participants a comprehensive understanding of how dynamical networks and uncertainty quantification interact. The practical capability is better reliability of conclusions: instead of reporting only one predicted outbreak, stability result, synchronization pattern, or cascade risk, an analyst can report how uncertain structure, parameters, and outside influences affect that conclusion. That supports decisions about what to measure next, which assumptions matter, and where a prediction should be treated cautiously.
976.limits: The input describes a three-hour tutorial, not a paper presenting one new tested method, so the abstract does not prove accuracy gains, provide datasets, or compare algorithms. Its usefulness depends on whether the uncertain pieces can be described honestly from data or expert knowledge. If the possible contact patterns, edge weights, transmission rates, demand changes, or outside shocks are badly guessed, the quantified uncertainty may look careful while still being misleading. It also assumes the chosen dynamic model captures the main way influence moves through the network. If the model leaves out a critical mechanism, measuring uncertainty inside that model will not fix the missing mechanism.

977.bp: Many useful data sets are graphs: people connected to friends, products connected to buyers, papers connected by citations, or web pages connected by links. A graph model learns from both the facts stored on each node and the pattern of connections around it. The problem is that real graphs can become too large to store, move, and train on cheaply. Graph condensation asks for a smaller substitute graph that can stand in for the original during learning. This paper serves that need by asking for a compressed graph that is not merely smaller, but still keeps the two things a graph model needs: node information and relationship structure. Its proposed DGC system turns many original nodes into reusable discrete codes, like a compact dictionary of node types, while also preserving high-order proximity, meaning similarity based on shared multi-step neighborhoods rather than only direct links. The goal is a small, informative graph that saves computation without erasing why nodes are related.
977.wh: The hard part is that graph information is spread across two surfaces at once. A node's features describe what the node is, while the graph structure describes where it sits and which other nodes can influence it. A small graph that preserves only node features may keep individual descriptions but lose the paths through which evidence travels. A small graph that preserves only local edges may miss broader neighborhood patterns, such as two nodes that are not directly connected but play similar roles because they reach similar surrounding nodes. Existing condensation methods also tend to create dense condensed representations, where many numbers must be stored and processed. Dense storage can be expensive, and it can carry extra noise because every tiny variation gets a place to live. The tension is compression versus faithfulness: the substitute must be much smaller, but it still has to behave like the original graph when a graph model learns from it.
977.naive: A smart beginner might sample a smaller set of nodes and edges from the original graph, then train on that subgraph. This is easy to understand, but it can throw away rare yet important regions and can break paths that explain why distant nodes have similar roles. Another beginner might cluster nodes by their feature values and keep one average node per group. That saves space, but it treats graph position as secondary, so nodes with similar attributes but very different neighborhoods may be merged incorrectly. A third attempt would store a dense compressed version of every condensed node. That keeps more detail, but it weakens the storage benefit and may preserve accidental noise along with useful signal.
977.ap: The paper's central move is to compress the graph in two coordinated ways. For structure, it looks beyond immediate neighbors and measures high-order proximity: nodes are close when their wider neighborhoods and multi-step connection patterns are similar. It then transfers this structural pattern into the condensed graph through low-rank approximation, which means keeping a small set of dominant structural directions instead of storing every pairwise detail. For node features, DGC discretizes them through a vector quantized variational autoencoder. In plain terms, the system learns a codebook of reusable feature codes, chooses codes that can represent many original nodes, and reconstructs useful information from those choices. This makes the condensed graph discrete rather than fully dense. The result is not just a tiny bag of node summaries; it is a compact graph whose codes and links are meant to preserve both what nodes look like and how they sit in the original network.
977.mech: The input is a large graph with node features and links. DGC first needs to decide what structural information matters. Instead of asking only whether two nodes share an edge, it uses high-order proximity, so the comparison includes broader neighborhoods reached through multiple steps. This captures role-like similarity: two nodes may matter in similar ways because information would flow to and from similar parts of the graph. The method then compresses this structural view with low-rank approximation. The everyday idea is that a huge table of relationships often contains repeated patterns; if a few main patterns explain most of the table, the system stores those main patterns and discards smaller fluctuations. That gives the condensed graph a structural backbone. In parallel, node features are passed through a vector quantized variational autoencoder. The encoder maps a node's features to a nearby entry in a learned codebook, so many nodes can share a discrete code. The decoder checks whether the chosen code can still recover the important feature information. During learning, the codebook and reconstruction process are adjusted so the discrete codes are useful, not arbitrary labels. The output is a smaller graph whose nodes are represented by codebook entries and whose structure is shaped to preserve the original graph's multi-step neighborhood patterns.
977.math: Several mathematical ideas are doing concrete jobs here. The first is graph proximity, which turns connection patterns into a notion of closeness. Direct proximity says two nodes are close if they touch; high-order proximity says they may also be close if their neighborhoods overlap or if short paths place them in similar graph roles. This fits the paper because graph models learn by moving evidence along links, so the important question is not only what a node says about itself, but what information can reach it. The second idea is low-rank approximation. A large relationship table can be viewed as many measurements of who is related to whom. If the table has repeated structure, it can be described by fewer hidden directions. Keeping those directions is a compression move: it saves structure while dropping smaller details that may be noise. The third idea is vector quantization, which replaces a continuous feature description with a discrete code selected from a codebook. The tradeoff is compression versus detail: shared codes reduce storage and redundancy, but they can blur differences between nodes. The variational autoencoder part adds a learn-and-reconstruct discipline: choose compact codes that still contain enough information to rebuild useful node features.
977.dots: This paper belongs to the graph learning and efficiency threads in the repository. It shares the same pressure as other compression work: large data structures can be too costly to train on directly, so the system needs a smaller proxy that keeps the training signal. It also connects to graph recommendation work such as DDGCL in the same batch, where low-rank approximation is used to keep broad interaction structure while reducing noise. The common idea is that graph relationships often contain repeated global patterns, not just isolated edges. It connects to adversarial graph and uncertainty work nearby because all of these papers ask when graph links can be trusted as evidence. DGC assumes links reveal useful structure worth preserving; attack papers ask how false links can exploit that assumption, while uncertainty work asks how predictions change when links or weights are noisy. The broader conference pattern is controlled information preservation: compress, perturb, retrieve, or defend graph evidence without losing the relationships that make it useful.
977.ww: DGC should improve over the naive approaches because it compresses the two graph ingredients in ways that match their natural shape. Structural information is not stored as a random subset of edges. It is summarized through high-order proximity, so the condensed graph can preserve broader neighborhoods and role similarity. This matters because graph models often benefit when a node receives evidence from related nodes, including nodes connected through short paths. Low-rank approximation helps because many large graphs contain repeated connection patterns: communities, hubs, common roles, and shared routes. Keeping the largest repeated patterns can preserve the structure most likely to guide learning while ignoring small variations that add cost. Discrete codes help on the feature side for a similar reason. Many nodes do not need entirely separate dense descriptions; they can share a learned code if the shared code keeps the important feature information. The codebook acts like a controlled vocabulary for node types. Together, these moves reduce storage and computation while making the compressed object resemble the original graph in the ways a graph model uses.
977.po: The payoff is a condensed graph that is designed to be smaller, more storage-efficient, and more structurally faithful than condensation methods focused mainly on features. The abstract reports experiments on multiple real-world graphs and comparison against nine baseline methods across different condensation ratios. The practical capability is that a graph model can be trained or tested against a much smaller substitute graph while retaining critical node information and multi-step structural patterns. If the method behaves as claimed, it buys cheaper graph learning without treating structure as an afterthought.
977.limits: The abstract supports the broad design but leaves several trust conditions open. DGC depends on high-order proximity being meaningful; if long-range neighborhoods mostly reflect noise, outdated links, or adversarial connections, preserving them may preserve the wrong signal. Discrete codes also assume many nodes can share feature patterns without losing task-relevant differences. If rare nodes matter precisely because they are unusual, codebook compression could blur them. Low-rank approximation assumes the graph's structure has repeated dominant patterns; graphs with many small, distinct local structures may compress less cleanly. The abstract reports experiments across ratios and baselines, but it does not show from this text which graph types, tasks, or failure cases are hardest.

978.bp: This paper is about a security problem in systems that reason over connected records. A graph neural network, or GNN, reads a map of objects and links: accounts linked by transactions, users linked by interactions, or items linked by relations. The model does not judge each object alone; it lets neighboring objects influence one another. That is useful, but it also creates an attack path. An adversary can add fake nodes and fake links so that evidence travels through the graph in a misleading way. The practical worry is strongest in security-sensitive domains, because a wrong graph decision may hide fraud, mislabel a risky account, or distort a protected decision. SoftHist studies graph injection attacks, where the attacker does not merely edit an existing node but inserts new graph material. The paper asks how such an attacker can work when the victim model is a black box, when graph choices are discrete, and when defenses are already watching for suspicious changes.
978.wh: The hard part is that the attacker has to satisfy several demands at once. The injected node must push the victim model toward misclassification, but it must also look plausible in the graph and survive defensive checks. Earlier graph injection methods often train a surrogate model, meaning a substitute model meant to imitate the hidden victim. That is tempting because it gives the attacker something to test against, but it can fail when the substitute behaves differently from the real target. The graph itself adds another obstacle. A node either has a feature, or it does not; an edge either exists, or it does not. Those yes-or-no choices make smooth adjustment difficult. The abstract also says existing attacks become much weaker against defended GNNs. So the attack is not just a search for harmful edits. It is a constrained search over discrete graph changes, with limited feedback, against a model and defenses the attacker cannot fully inspect.
978.naive: A smart beginner would first build a local copy of the target model, try many fake nodes against that copy, and then inject the best-looking ones into the real graph. They might connect the fake nodes to important targets and choose features that made the local copy misclassify. This fails in two ways described by the input data. First, the local copy can mismatch the real victim, so an attack that works in rehearsal may not work in deployment. Second, direct feature choice on a graph is awkward because the choices are discrete. Small changes do not behave like turning a dial; they jump from one valid graph state to another. A defended model adds a third failure: obvious or poorly shaped injections may be caught or neutralized.
978.ap: SoftHist turns the attack into repeated decision-making rather than a one-shot design problem. Instead of assuming the attacker owns a good copy of the victim model, it uses a gradient-free reinforcement learning approach, meaning it learns from trial outcomes without needing the victim model's internal slopes or parameters. The central move is to teach a policy, a rule for choosing attack actions, to add nodes, choose features, and sample edges in ways that increase misclassification while preserving camouflage. The paper adds three pieces for that purpose. A softened representation makes hard feature choices easier to explore before committing to valid graph features. A topology-aware edge sampler uses the shape of the graph when choosing connections. A defense-aware policy learner reuses adaptive history, so past attempts help guide future choices against defended models. The result is an attacker trained to balance harm, stealth, and defensive resistance.
978.mech: The mechanism starts with a target graph, a victim GNN that can be queried but not inspected, and an attack goal: make the model misclassify while inserting nodes that do not look obviously artificial. The learner treats each injection as a sequence of actions. It must decide what kind of fake node to create, what feature pattern that node should carry, and which existing nodes it should connect to. Because raw graph features are discrete, SoftHist temporarily uses a softened representation. In plain terms, it lets the learner consider graded mixtures of possible feature choices during search, reducing the chance that it gets stuck after an early bad yes-or-no decision. The topology-aware edge sampler then chooses candidate links with the graph structure in mind, rather than attaching fake nodes blindly. After an attempted injection, the black-box victim returns feedback through its classification behavior. The defense-aware policy learner uses that feedback as a score, favoring actions that cause misclassification while remaining stable and stealthy. Adaptive history reuse means earlier attack experiences are not discarded; they become memory about which actions worked under similar graph and defense conditions. What comes out is a set of injected nodes and edges selected by learned trial and correction, not by a hand-written attack recipe.
978.math: The main mathematical ideas are graph reasoning, sequential decision-making, and constrained search. In graph reasoning, each node is an object and each edge is a relationship that lets evidence move. The attack exploits the same assumption the victim model relies on: neighbors can influence how a node is judged. If an adversary can add a neighbor with carefully chosen features and links, the evidence arriving at a target node can be bent. Reinforcement learning is the decision math here. It asks: given the current graph state, what action should be taken next so later feedback is better? The action may be choosing a feature pattern or an edge. The reward is tied to misclassification, with the abstract indicating additional pressure for stealth and defense resistance. Gradient-free learning matters because the attacker does not depend on internal model derivatives, the small numerical directions many learning systems use to adjust themselves. Softened features are a relaxation: a hard choice is temporarily represented in a smoother form so search can compare nearby possibilities before returning to valid graph choices. The tradeoff is attack strength versus camouflage. A policy that only maximizes wrong labels may look suspicious; a policy that only hides may fail to change the prediction.
978.dots: This paper sits at the crossing of graph learning, security, and reinforcement learning. It is a graph paper because the attack works through nodes, links, and neighborhood structure, not through isolated records. It is a security paper because the useful question is not whether the model performs well on ordinary data, but whether it still behaves safely when someone shapes the input against it. It connects to the repo's broader privacy and security family, where useful sharing and connected learning create new attack surfaces. It also connects to recommendation shilling attacks and fake-news comment attacks in the same WSDM batch neighborhood: those papers likewise inject plausible-looking behavior or text to steer a model's output. The surface objects differ, but the shared problem is camouflage under strategic pressure. Compared with graph condensation or graph recommendation papers nearby, SoftHist uses graph structure in the opposite direction: not to make a useful model cheaper or better, but to reveal where connected reasoning can be manipulated.
978.ww: The method should improve over the naive approach because it learns from the actual attack setting instead of trusting a possibly wrong substitute model. If the victim is a black box, feedback from the victim's behavior is more honest than detailed information from a surrogate that may not match. Trial-and-error learning is slower, but it fits a setting where the attacker can observe whether a decision moved the target classification. The softened feature step helps because graph features are otherwise brittle. When every feature is a hard switch, early choices can trap the search in poor combinations. A softened intermediate form lets the learner compare alternatives more smoothly, then commit to valid injected features. The topology-aware sampler helps because links are not interchangeable. A fake node connected in an implausible place may be ineffective or detectable, while a node connected according to local graph shape can carry influence with less suspicion. The history component helps against defended models because defenses change which actions remain useful; remembering prior attempts gives the policy evidence about what has already failed or succeeded.
978.po: The payoff is a more realistic stress test for defended graph neural networks. According to the abstract and repo summaries, SoftHist avoids dependence on a surrogate model, handles discrete graph feature generation more stably, and explicitly aims at defended GNNs rather than undefended toy conditions. That buys an attack method that can search for fake nodes and edges under black-box feedback while balancing effectiveness, stealthiness, and resistance to defenses. For defenders, the value is also diagnostic: if a model can be fooled by such adaptive, topology-aware injections, then ordinary accuracy numbers are not enough to claim deployment safety.
978.limits: The abstract does not provide the full experimental evidence in this input, so the output cannot claim which datasets, defenses, or margins prove the result. The method assumes the attacker can query the victim enough times to learn useful feedback and that those queries do not themselves expose the attack. It also assumes softened feature search can be turned back into valid graph features without losing the attack signal. Topology-aware sampling depends on the visible graph structure being informative about plausible camouflage. Defense-aware history helps only when past attempts resemble future defended settings. A stronger or changing defense, stricter query limits, or graph domains with very unusual normal behavior could weaken the attack.

979.bp: Many useful questions are not answered by one stored fact. They are answered by walking through a structured map of facts. To discover co-authorship, a system may need to move from a paper to its authors and then to other papers. To support treatment selection, it may need to move from a symptom to a drug and then to prescriptions. The real task in this paper is retrieval over that kind of connected knowledge: given a downstream need, choose the facts, paths, or related objects that make the later task work. The difficulty is that the useful route through the structure is often implicit. People can notice a repeated relational pattern after experience, but a database usually does not arrive with every useful retrieval rule already written down. This paper asks how a system can discover those rules from feedback and use them to score structured retrieval results faithfully.
979.wh: The hard part is that structure helps only when the system follows the right kind of structure. A knowledge base can contain many relation chains, and most possible chains are not useful for a particular task. If the task is co-authorship discovery, the path paper to author to paper is meaningful. A longer path that wanders through venue, institution, and unrelated topic may also be legal in the graph but less faithful to the need. Rule writing is difficult because the useful patterns are rarely predefined, and different downstream tasks may need different paths. Feedback arrives after retrieval, so the system must infer which rule produced useful candidates rather than merely memorize one successful answer. The central tension is exploration versus control: the method must try possible relational rules, but it must also keep retrieval scores disciplined enough that accidental paths do not dominate.
979.naive: A smart beginner would ask domain experts to list useful paths, then score candidates that match those hand-written paths. That can work for familiar settings, but it fails when the task changes, the knowledge base is large, or the important pattern is not obvious before seeing feedback. Another beginner move is to retrieve by simple graph closeness, such as taking nearby nodes or short paths. That ignores relation meaning. A short path can be irrelevant, while a longer but semantically specific path can be exactly what the task needs. Both simple approaches treat rule discovery and retrieval scoring as separate problems, so a bad rule can guide scoring or a good scoring model can be starved of the right structural pattern.
979.ap: The paper's core move is to make rule discovery and retrieval scoring learn from each other. Instead of assuming that a human has already supplied the useful relational rules, the system searches for high-utility rules directly from downstream feedback. A rule here is a reusable path pattern through structured knowledge, such as moving from one type of object through one relation type to another. The system does not merely collect rules; it also learns how strongly each rule should affect retrieval scores. The abstract describes this as a two-level learning process. The upper level chooses candidate rules using reinforcement learning, which means it treats rule selection as repeated trial and feedback. The lower level trains the retrieval scorer under the guidance of the selected rules. By iterating, the system can discover rules that make retrieval better and adjust scoring so those rules are used in a measured way.
979.mech: The mechanism starts with a structured knowledge source, a downstream retrieval task, and feedback that says whether retrieved results helped that task. First, the system represents possible retrieval rules as structural patterns over relations. A candidate rule might say that useful evidence can be found by following relation A and then relation B, although the abstract gives examples rather than a formal rule language. Second, the upper-level module selects rules to try. Because it uses reinforcement learning, the selection is treated like choosing actions: pick a rule, observe downstream usefulness through retrieval feedback, and make future selections more likely when similar choices helped. Third, the lower-level retrieval module uses the selected rules to shape scoring functions. A scoring function is a learned measuring rule that assigns candidates larger or smaller values depending on how well they match the task and the discovered structure. Fourth, retrieval results are produced from those scores. Fifth, the downstream feedback flows back into the next round, so rule mining and scoring are not independent stages. The output is a set of learned retrieval rules and corresponding rule-guided scores, yielding retrieved structured knowledge for the downstream task. The abstract claims this loop reaches comparable performance to, and sometimes surpasses, systems that rely on manually specified rules.
979.math: The main mathematical object is a graph-like structure: objects are nodes, relation types are labeled links, and a rule is a pattern for walking through those links. The first mathematical idea is structured search. The number of possible paths can grow quickly, so the system needs a way to examine promising rule patterns without treating every path as equally plausible. The second idea is scoring. A score compresses several pieces of evidence into one number: whether a candidate follows a selected rule, how well it fits the task, and how useful similar choices have been. This compression is useful for ranking retrieved candidates, but it can hide why two candidates differ. The third idea is reinforcement learning, explained here as learning from consequences. The rule selector chooses a rule, receives feedback through downstream retrieval success, and shifts future choices toward rules with higher utility. The fourth idea is two-level optimization, meaning two connected searches happen at different levels. The upper search chooses rules; the lower search adjusts the scoring rule used for retrieval. The tradeoff is exploration versus reliability: try enough rules to find hidden structure, but constrain scoring so noisy or accidental paths do not become trusted evidence.
979.dots: This paper sits in the repo's Knowledge base retrieval theme because it treats retrieval as following meaningful structure, not just matching words. It also belongs near the knowledge-graphs family, where the repeated problem is deciding which links in a map of facts deserve trust. The connection to information retrieval is direct: the system still has to choose a small useful set from a large collection, but the candidates are shaped by relations and paths rather than plain documents alone. It connects to ranking because learned scores determine which structured candidates come first. It connects to optimization because both rule selection and scoring are adjusted from feedback. It also has a neighbor in reinforcement learning: selecting a retrieval rule is like choosing an action whose value is only known after seeing whether the downstream task benefits. The broader pattern is selective evidence movement: useful facts often sit two or more relation steps away, and the system must learn which routes carry meaning.
979.ww: The method should work better than a hand-written or closeness-only approach when downstream feedback contains repeated clues about useful relation patterns. If a certain path pattern keeps leading to good retrieval results, the upper-level selector can make that rule more likely. If a path looks common but does not help the task, feedback can reduce its influence. Joint learning matters because rules and scores depend on each other. A rule that is useful in principle may look weak if the scorer does not know how to value its matches. A scoring model may look good on surface features while missing the structural route that actually explains relevance. Coupling the two lets the system refine both sides: discover which patterns are worth following and learn how much their matches should count. This is especially natural for structured knowledge because relation patterns are reusable. Once the system learns that a path type matters for a task, the same rule can guide retrieval for many particular starting nodes, not just one memorized case.
979.po: The payoff is a retrieval system that does not require every useful structural rule to be manually specified before use. That matters in real knowledge bases, where downstream tasks can depend on hidden relational patterns that are hard for experts to enumerate completely. The abstract reports that the proposed unified rule mining and learning approach achieves comparable retrieval performance, matching or surpassing methods based on manually specified rules. Practically, this buys adaptability: the system can learn retrieval routes from feedback, attach scoring functions to those routes, and support structured downstream tasks with less dependence on prior rule engineering.
979.limits: Several assumptions must hold. The downstream feedback must be informative enough to distinguish a genuinely useful rule from a lucky path. The knowledge base must encode meaningful relation types; if links are missing, stale, too broad, or wrong, learned rules can faithfully amplify bad structure. The rule space must be expressive enough to contain useful patterns but controlled enough to search. The abstract does not specify the exact rule language, feedback signal, datasets, cost, or failure cases. It also does not prove that learned rules are interpretable to domain experts or that performance transfers across very different knowledge bases and tasks.

980.bp: A recommender is trying to decide which item should be shown to a person when the only direct evidence is past interaction: users clicked, bought, watched, skipped, or ignored items. Those interactions form a graph, meaning a map whose points are users and items and whose links are observed behavior. The useful signal is not only one user's history, but the larger pattern of which users and items sit near each other in that map. DDGCL serves this setting. It asks how to train a recommendation model when the training signal is created from the graph itself rather than from extra human labels. The practical pressure is especially clear for long-tail items, the rarely exposed items with too few interactions. If the system learns mostly from popular items, rare items stay poorly understood, get shown less often, and collect even less evidence. The paper tries to make self-created training comparisons preserve the graph's real structure while giving rare items stronger usable descriptions.
980.wh: The hard part is that the graph is both the evidence and the thing being changed during training. Many graph comparison methods create two altered versions of the same interaction graph, then train the model to agree across those versions. That can be useful because the model must learn what stays true when details vary. But if the alterations are random, they may delete exactly the links that make the graph meaningful. In recommendation, an edge is not a decorative detail; it may be the only sign that a user cared about an item. This is sharper for long-tail items because they have so few edges to begin with. Removing or corrupting one rare item's link can erase a large part of its evidence. The method therefore faces two tensions at once: create different views so learning has something to compare, but do not damage the structure that explains user-item preference; help rare items borrow global context, but do not pretend every rare item is just a copy of popular ones.
980.naive: A smart beginner might take the interaction graph, randomly drop some user-item links, randomly add noise, and ask the model to produce similar descriptions for the original and changed graphs. That creates cheap training pairs without labels. The failure is that randomness does not know which edges are disposable. A removed edge between a rare item and one of its few users may be more important than several edges around a popular item. Random changes can also distort communities of users and items, so the model learns to survive damage rather than learn the true preference structure. For long-tail items, a beginner might simply train longer or give them more weight. That still cannot invent reliable evidence if their local neighborhood remains thin.
980.ap: DDGCL's central move is to replace careless graph changes with diffusion-guided graph changes. Diffusion here means a controlled process that first adds noise to a structured object and then learns how to remove that noise, so the resulting view is different but still shaped by the original evidence. Before running this process, the paper uses singular value decomposition, a matrix tool that separates the largest broad patterns in the user-item interaction table from smaller details. This low-rank approximation, meaning a compressed version that keeps the strongest shared structure, gives the diffusion process a cleaner and cheaper base. The paper then adds a second diffusion route for long-tail items. Instead of asking rare items to stand on their tiny local evidence alone, a conditional diffusion model uses global graph information as guidance while denoising their descriptions. The result is dual: one part makes structure-preserving comparison views, and the other strengthens rare-item representations.
980.mech: The input is an interaction graph: users and items are points, and observed interactions are links. DDGCL first treats that graph as a matrix, where entries record whether or how users and items interacted. Singular value decomposition factors this matrix into broad directions of variation, which can be understood as major repeated patterns in the graph. Keeping a low-rank approximation means keeping the strongest patterns while discarding some fine detail. This compressed graph is not the final answer; it is the base used to speed and guide the next stage. The contrastive view optimization module then runs a diffusion process on this base. It adds noise, learns to reverse the noise, and produces alternative graph views that differ enough to create a useful comparison but are constrained by the graph's broad structure. The recommendation model learns from these views by making descriptions of matching views agree and nonmatching cases separate, so it is trained by comparison rather than by hand labels. For long-tail items, the paper adds embedding augmentation, where an embedding is a learned numeric description of an item. A conditional diffusion model denoises these rare-item descriptions while being guided by global graph information. The output is a set of learned user and item descriptions that should preserve structural relations and give rare items a better basis for ranking.
980.math: The paper combines four mathematical ideas. The first is graph reasoning: represent users and items as points connected by behavior, then assume that nearby or similarly connected points carry useful evidence about each other. This fits recommendation because preference is rarely visible from one action; it appears through repeated relations among many users and items. The second idea is matrix compression through singular value decomposition. A user-item graph can be stored as a large table. SVD finds broad axes that explain many entries in that table, so a low-rank approximation keeps the main skeleton while reducing incidental detail and computation. The third idea is diffusion, a probability-based way to learn what structured noise looks like and how to remove it. Here the uncertain object is a graph view or rare-item description: the model learns to perturb it without losing the signal that should remain. The fourth idea is contrastive learning, a comparison rule that pulls two trustworthy views of the same underlying object closer and pushes mismatched objects apart. The tradeoff is structure versus variation. Too little variation teaches nothing; too much variation breaks the meaning of the graph.
980.dots: This paper sits at the crossing of several recurring conference ideas in the repo's current map. It belongs to recommender systems because the final job is ranking items for users when only a small set can be shown. It belongs to graph learning because the evidence is relational: a user-item link matters partly because of neighboring users, neighboring items, and larger connectivity patterns. It also belongs to self-supervised contrastive work because the training signal is manufactured from comparisons between views, not supplied as a new human label. The diffusion part connects it to generative and denoising papers that try to create useful variants without destroying the object being modeled. The long-tail part connects it to ranking and exposure-bias problems across recommendation: popular items receive abundant feedback, rare items stay uncertain, and the system's past choices shape future data. DDGCL's specific niche is using global graph structure to make comparison views and rare-item augmentation less arbitrary.
980.ww: The approach should work when the global structure of the interaction graph is more stable than any single observed edge. Random augmentation treats all graph details as equally safe to change. DDGCL instead tries to identify the broad skeleton first, then lets diffusion vary the graph around that skeleton. That gives the model a better lesson: two views can be different in surface details while still preserving the same user-item preference structure. The comparison training then rewards descriptions that capture the preserved structure rather than the random accident of one edge. For long-tail items, the conditional diffusion module helps because rare items often share larger graph patterns with better-observed items. A niche product may have few clicks, but the users who clicked it may resemble users around related products, and its position in the graph may still carry context. Guiding denoising with global graph information lets the rare item borrow statistical strength without directly fabricating interactions. The method improves over the naive approach by controlling what information is allowed to change and what must stay anchored.
980.po: The payoff is a recommendation model that can train on self-created graph views without relying on destructive random changes. According to the abstract and repo metadata, DDGCL is meant to preserve graph structural information, accelerate diffusion through SVD-based low-rank approximation, and improve representation learning for long-tail items. In practical terms, that buys two capabilities: better use of the existing interaction graph and better treatment of items with insufficient exposure. If the claims hold, the recommender should be less biased toward only the items with abundant feedback and more capable of ranking rare items from their relation to the whole graph.
980.limits: The method assumes the interaction graph contains real reusable structure. If links mainly reflect old exposure bias, promotion, bots, or accidental visibility, preserving global structure can preserve the wrong signal. The low-rank compression must keep the patterns that matter; if rare-item clues live in small details, compression may weaken them. The diffusion views must be faithful enough that positive comparisons really describe the same preference structure. The abstract does not prove how the method behaves under changing catalogs, new users, adversarial manipulation, or domains where rare items are genuinely unlike popular ones. It also does not show from the abstract alone how much of the gain comes from diffusion, SVD, or long-tail augmentation separately.

981.bp: A large recommendation system has to choose items from a catalog that is too big to scan by hand or describe with simple labels. Newer generative recommenders do this by producing a compact item code, called a semantic ID, instead of directly naming every possible item. The code is useful only if it carries the kinds of meaning that matter for ranking: what the content is about, how creators relate through shared audiences, and what language-based understanding says about the item. RankID serves that problem. The paper asks how to make one usable ID when the evidence arrives in different forms, or modalities: content-understanding features, creator-level co-engagement information, and semantic information from multiple features. SEALNet is presented as the alignment machinery, and RankID is the task-specific output for large-scale recommendation systems.
981.wh: The difficulty is that each feature source speaks a different practical language. A content-understanding feature may describe what an item looks like or means. Creator-level co-engagement says something different: audiences who engage with the same creators reveal social and behavioral neighborhoods. Language-model-derived features can add broader semantic hints, but those hints are not automatically compatible with behavior signals. A simple merger can make one source dominate or can mix signals whose meanings do not line up. The result may be a semantic ID that is compact but confused: it may group items together because they share surface content while missing creator-audience patterns, or it may follow co-engagement while losing the actual content meaning. The paper is hard because the ID must be unified enough for generation, specific enough for ranking, and flexible enough to support different recommendation tasks.
981.naive: A smart beginner would collect all available features for an item, paste them together into one long description, and train a recommender to turn that description into a semantic ID. That sounds reasonable because more evidence should help. The failure is that adding evidence is not the same as aligning evidence. If content features, creator co-engagement, and language-derived signals occupy incompatible coordinate systems, their raw combination can blur rather than clarify meaning. Another naive route is to build separate IDs for each feature type, but then the generative recommender must decide among several vocabularies. That defeats the purpose of having one compact code the system can generate consistently at scale.
981.ap: The central move is to make semantic ID construction an alignment problem before it is a coding problem. SEALNet, as described in the abstract, learns to align and integrate the semantics of diverse input features. In plain terms, it tries to translate different evidence sources into a shared meaning map before compressing them into an ID. RankID then uses that shared map to build task-specific IDs for large recommendation systems. The two examples show the design. RankID-Graph starts with a content-understanding feature and enriches it with creator-level co-engagement, so an item's code reflects both what the system sees in the content and which creators share audience behavior. RankID-LLM integrates semantic information from multiple features into a single SID, so the final code can be generated as one item language rather than several disconnected descriptions.
981.mech: The input is one item with several feature descriptions attached to it. Some features describe content directly. Some describe relationships around creators, especially co-engagement, where users engaging with the same creators provide evidence that those creators or their items may occupy nearby recommendation neighborhoods. Other features carry semantic information produced or organized through language-model-style understanding. The mechanism first treats these sources as different views of the same recommendation object, not as interchangeable columns. SEALNet learns alignments among them, meaning it learns how evidence from one view should correspond to evidence from another when both are trying to describe the item's useful meaning. After alignment, the system integrates the views into a unified representation, a compact learned description whose parts are meant to be comparable across items. RankID then turns that integrated description into a semantic ID suited to a recommendation task. In the graph version, creator co-engagement enriches content features before ID construction, so audience relations can correct or supplement content-only meaning. In the LLM version, several semantic feature sources are folded into one ID. The output is not a human label. It is a generated code that the recommender can use as the item-side vocabulary for ranking or retrieval.
981.math: The main mathematical idea is alignment: take several descriptions of the same object and learn a transformation that makes their meanings comparable. In everyday terms, alignment is like putting several maps of the same city on the same scale before combining them. If one map marks roads, another marks foot traffic, and another marks neighborhoods, overlaying them without adjustment creates nonsense. SEALNet's role is to learn the adjustment from data rather than hand-write it. A second idea is representation, meaning the item is squeezed into a short numeric or discrete description that preserves the distinctions useful for recommendation. This creates a compression tradeoff: the ID must be small enough to generate over a large catalog, but rich enough not to erase useful differences. A third idea is graph evidence. In RankID-Graph, creators and shared engagement form a relationship map; links matter because users who co-engage with creators reveal behavioral similarity that content alone may miss. Finally, ranking pressure sits behind the whole design. A semantic ID is valuable because it helps sort candidate items for users. The math fits because recommendation needs comparable, compact item codes built from partial, uneven evidence.
981.dots: This paper connects directly to the recommender-systems family in the repo: many papers are trying to choose useful items from huge catalogs when clicks, content, language, images, and graph relations each provide incomplete evidence. It is closest to the semantic-ID branch. DOS also treats semantic IDs as a foundation for generative recommendation and worries that the code space must match the generation task. SID-Coord coordinates ordinary item identifiers with semantic IDs for short-video ranking, which is another version of balancing memorization with meaning-based generalization. The SID staleness paper asks what happens when interaction-informed IDs drift over time. RankID focuses on a different pressure: before the ID can become stale or be coordinated with other IDs, it must first combine heterogeneous multimodal features coherently. Conceptually, it sits at the intersection of similarity, ranking, graph reasoning, language-model recommendation, and information compression.
981.ww: The approach should improve over naive feature mixing because it respects the fact that different evidence sources can be useful for different reasons. Content understanding can say what an item appears to be. Creator co-engagement can say how audiences behave around related creators. Language-based semantic features can add broader meaning that may not be visible from interaction counts alone. If these are simply concatenated, the model has to discover both translation and recommendation at once, and strong or noisy features can swamp weaker but important ones. Multi-stage semantic alignment breaks the job into a cleaner sequence: first make the views speak a shared language, then integrate them, then produce a task-specific ID. That helps because a unified ID can carry agreement among sources while still allowing each RankID variant to emphasize the evidence its task needs. The graph variant works by letting audience relationships enrich content meaning. The LLM variant works by folding multiple semantic signals into one generatable code.
981.po: The payoff is a more unified item-code layer for generative recommendation. Grounded in the abstract, RankID buys the ability to generate semantic IDs across heterogeneous multimodal features instead of maintaining disconnected IDs for each feature source. RankID-Graph can enrich content understanding with creator-level co-engagement, which should help when content alone misses audience structure. RankID-LLM can combine semantic information from multiple features into one SID, which gives the recommender a single compact code to use at scale. The practical capability is not merely better description; it is making the generated item vocabulary more usable for ranking.
981.limits: Several assumptions must hold. The feature sources must contain complementary signal, not just duplicate or contradictory noise. Creator co-engagement must reflect meaningful audience relationships rather than exposure patterns caused by platform layout, creator popularity, or promotion. Language-derived semantic features must describe item meaning in a way that matches recommendation goals. The abstract names SEALNet and two RankID implementations, but it does not specify the training objective, datasets, evaluation metrics, latency cost, or failure cases. It also does not prove that one unified ID preserves minority tastes, avoids popularity bias, or remains stable when content, creators, and user behavior change over time.

982.bp: The ordinary system behind this paper is a social-media news detector that judges not only an article but also the surrounding user reaction. In a feed, comments are part of the evidence: they can make a story look discussed, doubted, supported, or treated as ordinary by readers. Fake-news detectors therefore may read comments along with the article and use those patterns to decide whether the post looks false or real. This paper asks what happens when the comment stream itself becomes an attack channel. Instead of changing the article, an attacker appends comments that look like plausible human reactions but are chosen to push the detector toward the wrong label. The need is defensive: if platforms trust detectors that can be moved by added comments, then an attacker can influence automated moderation while leaving the original article mostly untouched. The paper studies that weak point by combining explanation of a detector's decision with language-model comment generation.
982.wh: The hard part is that the attack must satisfy two audiences at once. It must affect the detector, which may rely on small word patterns across article and comments, and it must remain believable to humans, because awkward or unrelated comments would be easy to filter or doubt. Prior comment attacks described in the abstract have two weaknesses. Some generate synthetic text that can be unrealistic, so they may not resemble normal social-media responses. Others retrieve existing comments, but without knowing which parts of those comments matter to the detector. That means they may add text that looks natural but has little effect, or text that changes the wrong signal. The defender's system is also not a single target: the paper evaluates against dEFEND, TextCNN, and RoBERTa, which implies different ways of reading content and interactions. A useful attack has to be targeted enough to move model decisions while general enough to remain credible across detectors.
982.naive: A smart beginner attacker would try one of two simple plans. The first is to ask a language model to write many supportive or doubtful comments and append them to the article until the detector changes its mind. That fails because natural-sounding text is not automatically strategically useful; the detector may ignore most of it. The second plan is to copy comments from similar news posts. That can sound more human, but it is unguided. It treats every plausible comment as equally useful even though the detector may depend on particular words or word pieces. Both plans miss the key question: which small parts of the combined article-and-comment evidence are actually driving the fake-or-real score?
982.ap: The core move is to turn the detector's own explanation into an attack recipe. The paper uses SHAP, an explanation method that estimates how much each input piece contributes to a model's decision by comparing the prediction with and without that piece across many partial versions of the input. In plain terms, it asks: which words or word pieces are carrying the most weight for the fake or real label? Those influential pieces become instructions for a large language model, which is a text generator trained to continue and rewrite language in human-like form. The generator is prompted to produce contextually credible comments that include the influential pieces. The comments are then appended to the article. The attack is therefore neither random generation nor blind copying. It is guided by the detector's sensitive features, but wrapped in language that should look like ordinary user reaction.
982.mech: The mechanism starts with a news article and a target fake-news detector. The detector reads the article, and in systems that use social context it may also read user comments or interaction text. First, the attack obtains an explanation of the detector's current decision. SHAP assigns contribution scores to input pieces, meaning it estimates which words or word fragments most increased or decreased the detector's belief that the article is fake or real. The attacker then selects influential pieces that are useful for moving the decision in the desired direction. Next, those pieces are placed into a prompt for a large language model. The prompt does not merely ask for any comment; it asks for a comment that fits the article context and naturally uses the selected high-impact pieces. The language model outputs one or more human-like comments. These generated comments are appended to the article, making them part of the evidence the detector sees. The modified article-plus-comments input is then submitted to detectors such as dEFEND, TextCNN, and RoBERTa. The score being tested is whether the detector's fake-or-real classification changes or weakens compared with the original input. Finally, the attack is compared with MALCOM, CopyCat, and retrieval-based comment attacks, so the output is not just a fooled detector but evidence about whether explanation-guided generation is more effective than earlier comment strategies.
982.math: The main mathematical idea is contribution scoring under uncertainty. A detector produces one final label, but that label is made from many small signals. SHAP borrows from cooperative game theory, where the question is how much credit each participant deserves for a team outcome. Here the participants are input pieces, and the outcome is the detector's fake-or-real score. The method estimates a piece's value by asking how the score changes when that piece is present across many possible partial inputs. This is not proof that a word caused the detector's decision in the human sense; it is an accounting method for model dependence. The second idea is targeted search in language. The attacker has a constraint: produce text that contains useful high-impact pieces while still sounding like a normal comment. A large language model supplies a probability-based continuation rule, choosing likely next words from patterns learned in text, while the prompt constrains what evidence must appear. The third idea is adversarial evaluation: change the input in a small, allowed way and measure whether the output label changes. The tradeoff is precision versus realism. Purely strategic text may be unnatural; purely natural text may be harmless. The paper's math-guided generation tries to keep both.
982.dots: This paper sits in the conference's misinformation and trust family, but on the attack side rather than the defense side. It connects to sentiment-manipulation work such as AdSent because both expose a detector that may rely on a shortcut: emotional wording in one case, influential comment words in this case. It also connects to robust fake-news detection work such as LLM-TKT, where the concern is that LLM-generated injections can pollute the signals used by graph or propagation-based detectors. The shared problem is that trust systems often treat surrounding text as useful social evidence, but attackers can manufacture that surrounding evidence. It also touches the explainability and interpretability thread: an explanation tool meant to help humans inspect a model can become a map for attacking the model. The broader lesson is that retrieval, generation, explanation, and detection are no longer separate pieces. Once attackers can generate fluent comments and read model sensitivities, fake-news detection becomes an arms race over which evidence is trustworthy.
982.ww: The approach should work because it attacks the detector at the level where the detector actually makes its mistake. A blind generated comment hopes that enough extra text will shift the score. An explanation-guided comment uses the detector's own sensitivity map to choose words or word pieces that the detector already treats as important. That makes the added text more likely to move the decision than a generic reaction would. The large language model matters for a different reason: it hides the strategic pieces inside ordinary comment form. If the selected pieces were simply pasted as a keyword list, a filter or reader could notice the manipulation. If they appear inside a plausible human response to the article, the modified input can satisfy the detector's text patterns without looking obviously artificial. The method also benefits from preserving the article itself. Because the attack adds comments rather than rewriting the news content, it avoids some visible changes that article-text attacks might introduce. Its advantage comes from combining two weak tools into one stronger one: explanation supplies targeting, and generation supplies believable wording.
982.po: The payoff is a clearer warning about a new attack surface for fake-news detectors. The abstract claims that comment-based attacks have been underexplored and that this approach is competitive with existing generative, CopyCat, MALCOM, and retrieval-based attacks. In practical terms, the paper shows that a detector can be pressured not only by changing the article but by manipulating the surrounding conversation. That matters for platform safety because comments are cheap to create, easy to append, and often treated as social context. The result gives defenders a concrete failure mode to test: whether their detectors over-trust comments that contain influential but attacker-chosen language.
982.limits: The abstract is truncated, so it does not reveal the full reported numbers, datasets, success rates, or human realism tests. The claim also depends on SHAP explanations being faithful enough to identify genuinely influential input pieces; if the explanation scores are noisy, the attack guidance may be weak. The method assumes the attacker can append comments to the article context seen by the detector and can query or inspect enough model behavior to run explanation-guided selection. It is evaluated against named detectors, but the abstract does not prove the same effect for every moderation system, every language, every platform rule, or detectors trained specifically to discount suspicious comment injections.

983.bp: News believability is not controlled only by whether an article is wholly true or wholly fabricated. Readers also react to small signals inside the wording: whether a claim sounds certain or cautious, whether a cause is presented as proven or merely possible, whether an inconvenient qualifying fact remains in view, and whether contrary evidence is introduced. This paper studies that middle zone. The object being manipulated is a political news story that mostly remains the same, but whose credibility cues are changed by a large language model, meaning a system trained to produce fluent text from patterns in large text collections. The practical worry is that cheap, polished editing lets an attacker shift belief without writing an obviously fake story. Instead of asking whether machines can invent news from nothing, the paper asks whether they can make small, low-visibility edits that move human judgments of believability while preserving the core input story.
